sources.title: Ibrahim Muteferrika (Q561445), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-05): English label 'İbrahim Müteferrika', description 'Ottoman polymath', Korean label 이브라힘 뮈테페리카, born 1674 (also given as 1670), died 1745 (also given as 1747), citizenship Ottoman Empire, place of birth Cluj-Napoca, place of death Istanbul. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi (Turkish Diyanet Foundation Encyclopaedia of Islam), entry 'Ibrahim Muteferrika' (vol. 21; entry cited in the scholarly literature as by Erhan Afyoncu), read in full in Turkish. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: born at Kolozsvar (Cluj) between about 1670 and 1674, with his original name and family unknown; the older legend of a captured Calvinist student sold in the Istanbul slave market is refuted by Niyazi Berkes, who shows he came from a Unitarian background; his career as sipahi, court muteferrika, interpreter and liaison to Ferenc Rakoczi from 1717, and court historiographer from 1744; permission in July 1727, by decree of Ahmed III and a fatwa of the Seyhulislam, to found the first Turkish printing press, which he ran from his house after Mehmed Said Efendi withdrew; 17 books (23 volumes) printed until his death, interrupted only for about a year by the Patrona Halil revolt and slowed by his state duties; first print runs of 1,000-1,200 copies fell to 500, partly because the books did not sell; his own pamphlet on the usefulness of printing (cheaper, clearer, error-free books, large libraries, and keeping Europe's printing trade money at home); his additions and maps (Marmara 1720, Black Sea 1724-25, Iran 1729-30, Egypt) and his additions to Katib Celebi's Cihannuma on post-Renaissance astronomy, 'the most important text on the subject in Turkish for a century'; the paper mill he attempted at Yalova with workers brought from Poland; and the 1745 versus 1747 death-date problem (a tombstone and pay record favour 6 February 1747). Scholarly encyclopaedia, Turkish-language; the strongest single source, with a critical register on sales and delays.

Orlin Sabev (Orhan Salih), 'Portrait and Self-Portrait: Ibrahim Muteferrika's Mind Games' (Osmanli Arastirmalari / The Journal of Ottoman Studies, peer-reviewed article with an English text), read in full from the journal's PDF: a critical cross-reading of the only three narratives of his life, namely his own 1710 treatise and the reports of two contemporaries, the Hungarian nobleman Cesar de Saussure (letter of 21 February 1732: 'smart and clever', learned the Turks' language and law, expressed the wish to introduce arts and sciences and suggested a printing shop to the Grand Vizier, who approved and funded it) and the French liaison Charles de Peyssonnel (1738: 'a very good man', 'the spirit of the project, hardworking rather than skillful', retaining some Latin); the argument that his own account of his conversion may be a flattering self-portrait written for the sultan; and evidence that he was publicly known as 'Ibrahim Efendi the Printer', including his 1747 probate inventory. Peer-reviewed independent scholarship; the private-religion material is deliberately not used here.

Uskudar University, biography page 'Ibrahim Muteferrika', read in full: Hungarian-origin printer, publisher, author and translator (1674-1745); his languages and role in delegations; the role of Mehmed Said Efendi, who had seen a Paris printing house, and of Grand Vizier Damat Ibrahim Pasha; permission for non-religious works only and a fatwa; the press, named Daru't-Tibaati'l Amire, established 16 December 1727 with machines and Latin type bought abroad and Arabic type of uncertain source; the Yalova paper mill; 17 works in history, geography and dictionaries; later fate of the press. University biography, celebratory; its figures differ slightly from the encyclopaedia (22 rather than 23 volumes; death 1745).

Jeremy Norman's History of Information, 'Printer Ibrahim Muteferrika Issues the First Book Printed by Muslims Using Movable Type' (reference page built on the Indiana University copy of the 1729 Vankulu Lugati), read in full: according to Ottoman documents he cut his own punches and cast his own Arabic type during the two years before the first book; the dictionary in two volumes of 666 and 756 pages; the imperial decree and religious rulings reproduced at the front of the book; and his pamphlet 'The Usefulness of Printing' presented to the Grand Vizier, listing ten reasons for an imperial press. Specialist reference page by a bibliographic historian; some phrasing ('first Muslim printer') is the page's own claim.

Daily Sabah, opinion article 'Converting to Ottoman world: First Muslim printer, Ibrahim Muteferrika' (Turkish daily, opinion column), read in full: his Cluj and Unitarian background, his rise through court service and diplomacy, the 1727 press with Said Efendi, the first book (Vankulu), the interruption by the 1730 revolt and the grand mufti's endorsement; his authorship (a treatise on Islam, a treatise on state and military order, and the pamphlet on printing); his argument that print would make books widespread and allow great libraries; and the claim that printing stopped after his death for economic reasons because sales were poor. Opinion piece in a government-aligned newspaper, strongly admiring ('the Ottoman Enlightenment' framing is the writer's own); used as a perspective, not as a behavioural source.

Ekrem Bugra Ekinci, 'Myths and Reality about the Printing Press in the Ottoman Empire' (article on the author's site), read in full: earlier Greek, Armenian and Jewish presses in Ottoman lands, the pamphlet's reasoning, the Seyhulislam's fatwa permitting printing of non-religious books and the firman of December 1727, the company formed with Said Efendi and the four proofreaders hired, the 'two maps and 21 volumes' printed, his work as publisher, and a claim that about 70 percent of his copies sold before his death, which contradicts the poor-sales account in the other sources. Revisionist article by an Ottoman historian defending the press against 'bigotry' myths; claims about sales are the author's and conflict with TDV.

persistence.rationale: [src_mut_tdv, src_mut_sabev, src_mut_uskudar, src_mut_dailysabah | 1726-1747 | scholarly encyclopaedia + peer-reviewed article + university page + opinion column] TDV records that he ran the press until his death, printing 17 works in 23 volumes with only about a year of interruption during the 1730 revolt, even though his duties for the state repeatedly slowed it, print runs fell from 1,000-1,200 to 500 and books sold poorly; Uskudar University and the TDV also describe the Yalova paper mill he tried to establish; Peyssonnel's 1738 description, quoted by Sabev, calls him 'hardworking rather than skillful'. The continuation is documented by a scholarly encyclopaedia and corroborated by contemporaries; how much was personal tenacity rather than state support is not separable.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_mut_sabev, src_mut_tdv, src_mut_norman, src_mut_uskudar | 1720s | peer-reviewed article quoting a contemporary + encyclopaedia + reference page + university page] Saussure's 1732 letter, quoted by Sabev, says he suggested a printing shop to the Grand Vizier, who approved and advanced the funds; Norman and TDV record his written case ('The Usefulness of Printing', ten reasons) and the permissions obtained from the sultan and the chief jurist; TDV and Uskudar add that the press stood in his own house and that he later tried a paper mill, and Norman says that, according to Ottoman documents, he cut his own punches and cast his own Arabic type (Uskudar says the source of the Arabic type is uncertain). Against this, Uskudar and the Daily Sabah column credit Mehmed Said Efendi with the first impulse after seeing a Paris printing house, so the initiative was shared. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): top-risk row; lowered from 70 / 0.52 to 66 / 0.48 because the 'he suggested it' claim rests on one contemporary letter and the other sources credit a partner with starting the project.

persuasiveness.rationale: [src_mut_norman, src_mut_tdv, src_mut_ekinci | 1726-1727 | reference page + encyclopaedia + historian's article] Norman says he wrote a pamphlet listing ten reasons for an imperial press and presented it to the Grand Vizier; TDV summarises its arguments (cheap, clear, error-free books, large libraries, money kept at home) and the decree and fatwa that followed; Ekinci quotes the jurist's fatwa permitting the printing of non-religious books. The permissions were obtained with conditions (no religious books) and with a powerful partner, and no source says his argument was decisive. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): top-risk row; lowered from 62 / 0.48 to 58 / 0.44 because the sources show a written appeal and an outcome but not that his persuasion, rather than the vizier's own interest and Said Efendi's backing, produced the permission.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_mut_tdv, src_mut_uskudar, src_mut_norman | 1720-1745 | scholarly encyclopaedia + university page + reference page] TDV lists four maps he translated or drew and printed (Marmara, Black Sea, Iran, Egypt), the additions he made to Katib Celebi's geography on post-Renaissance European astronomy (called the most important Turkish text on the subject for a century), the dictionary, history, geography and military titles he chose to print, and the paper mill; Norman adds that he made his own Arabic type; Uskudar adds printing and calligraphy training. The combination of printing technology, cartography, scientific commentary and publishing is documented in one strong source and a few corroborating ones. His religious treatise, his treatise on state and military order, and his diplomatic and interpreting work are context and not used for this row.

portrait.reason: Portrait HELD on sitter identity (after a holder-record and plate-lettering check). The Rijksmuseum catalogues print RP-P-1905-4876 (Gilles Edme Petit, Paris, 1742; Public Domain Mark and CC0) as 'Portret van Ibrahim Muteferrika', but the plate's own lettering reads 'Seid Achmet Aga Muteferrica Guedikli Zaim de Boziazi ... Grand Marechal de l'Ambassade en France'. That names a different man, an Ottoman embassy officer in Paris, and 'Muteferrica' there is the court title; the printer served in Istanbul and no source read says he travelled to France, so the museum's identification (and its 'dedicated to Ibrahim Muteferrika' note) is contradicted by the inscription. The rights themselves were clear. The only other images found are photographs of a modern statue and bust in Istanbul (derivative sculptures with their own rights; the Wikidata image is one of them), a modern seal photo and a Cyrillic script graphic; no contemporary or otherwise rights-clear likeness of the printer was found, and the scholarly article read describes only verbal portraits of him. Next step: a source that positively identifies an early depiction of him with a clear holder statement, or a rights-cleared modern illustration commissioned for the site.

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: STRONG (lead-robust) (lead) / FAILED ON IDENTITY: the lead's Rijksmuseum print (RP-P-1905-4876, Petit, Paris 1742) has Public Domain Mark and CC0 rights, but the downloaded scan carries the lettering 'Seid Achmet Aga Muteferrica Guedikli Zaim de Boziazi, Fief du premier Ordre, en Asie un des grands Officiers et Ecuyer de main de sa Hautesse et Grand Marechal de l'Ambassade en France' and 'Presente par son tres humble Serviteur Petit 1742'; the sitter is a different Ottoman official (an embassy officer; Muteferrica is a court title, not the printer's name); the museum's own record lists that lettering as the second title but its main title and 'dedicated to' note name Ibrahim Muteferrika. The Roster64 Zeno lesson applied: the inscription decides. Checked: Commons category (the P18 image is a photo of a statue, a seal photo and a script graphic) and the museum record; no other lead. Portrait therefore HELD (see portrait.reason); all research kept. BIRTH/DEATH: TDV says born between about 1670 and 1674; I use 1674 (Wikidata first value, Uskudar, Norman). Death: TDV and Sabev's probate inventory (1 April 1747) and a pay record (6 February 1747) support 1747, over the 1745 chronogram date, so deathYear 1747. ZERO POLITICS: primary identity printer, publisher and scholar; his diplomatic and interpreter service (liaison to Rakoczi, the Orsova negotiations, missions to Poland and Dagestan), the treatise on state and military reform and the religious treatise are context and not scored. EXCLUSIONS: the circumstances and motives of his conversion (the sources conflict and it is a private religious matter; Sabev's reading of a possibly flattering self-portrait is not used to infer personality), family and health. VOCABULARY: occupations scholar, editor and entrepreneur (no printer or publisher id exists), fields technology and education, tags founder and innovator, archetype entrepreneurial_builder, impact domains technological, cultural and educational, all grepped in en.ts and ko.ts. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: TDV Islam Ansiklopedisi entry (https://islamansiklopedisi.org.tr/ibrahim-muteferrika). READ (substantive): TDV encyclopaedia entry in Turkish (biography); Sabev peer-reviewed article with the Saussure and Peyssonnel contemporary accounts (biography); Uskudar University page (institution); Jeremy Norman's History of Information page (archive); Daily Sabah opinion column (press); Ekinci article on press myths (press). 6 sources plus Wikidata for the QID; also read but not used as support: an essay on icraa.org (authorship unclear) correcting the label 'first Turkish printing press', and a University of Utah library blog tag page. PERSPECTIVES: (1) scholarly encyclopaedia; (2) peer-reviewed critical article quoting two contemporaries; (3) university and reference pages; (4) two admiring or revisionist newspaper/opinion pieces that disagree with the scholarly sources on sales. NON-SELF BEHAVIOURAL SOURCES: TDV and Sabev (including the quoted Saussure and Peyssonnel reports). COUNTER-VOICES: TDV on slow sales and shrinking print runs; Sabev's critical reading; Ekinci's contradicting claim. His own writings (the pamphlet, the treatises) were not opened, only described by the sources; self-report is therefore limited to the pamphlet's arguments as summarised by TDV and Norman. NOT OPENED: Sabev's 2025 book 'The Muteferrika Press' (only the publisher's description), Britannica (bot wall), Cambridge History of the Book excerpt (503), the Oxford and Cambridge studies by Berkes, Watson and Afyoncu themselves. DISCREPANCIES: permission July 1727 (TDV) vs December 1727 (firman per Ekinci and Uskudar); 17 works in 23 volumes (TDV) vs 22 volumes (Uskudar) vs 21 volumes and two maps (Ekinci); first print runs 1,000-1,200 (TDV, Ekinci 1,000); sales: poor (TDV, Daily Sabah) vs about 70 percent sold (Ekinci); 'first Turkish press' contested because non-Muslim presses existed in Ottoman lands earlier. Sparse pre-modern profile, confidence capped at 0.52. SCORING: 4 rows (cross_domain_range 66/0.50, proactive_agency 66/0.48, persistence 64/0.52, persuasiveness 58/0.44).
